Researchers have shed light on a curious group of bacteria that use iron in much the same way that animals use oxygen: to soak up electrons during biochemical reactions.

Some relevant background: We know of many bacteria that use elements besides oxygen in this way. While oxygen is our most familiar terminal electron acceptor, other compounds can fill this role in certain niches, conditions, and/or bacterial strains. Some bacteria reduce nitrates, others sulfates, and others iron. This way they can live in oxygen-free environments, and in many cases oxygen is actively toxic to these bacteria.

The paper's pretty dense, but they used culture techniques and genetic analysis to study this microbial community, determining that indeed, these microbes (which are not easily reared in the lab and don't grow alone) convert one iron form, Fe3+ to the other Fe2+, during metabolism.

The big finding seems to be that this reduction reaction seems to be going on outside of the bacterial cells, meaning that somehow the electrons generated in microbial metabolism are being shuttled outside of the cells to react with the Fe3+ without importing it into the cells. Source
